newsitem.title: USA: No special session in Colorado over tax refund.
newsitem.headline: No special session in Colorado over tax refund.

text.p: Colorado Gov. Roy Romer on Tuesday said he will not call a special session of the legislature to write a ballot item that would have asked voters to approve spending an estimated $140 million state surplus.
In effect, the money, which comes out to about $80 per taxpayer, will be returned to them.
Romer, a Democrat, said there was no support in the Republican controlled legislature for calling the special session.
The governor had hoped to call the special session to write a question for November's ballot that would ask voters if they wanted refunds or have the state spend the excess on schools and roads.
He chided lawmakers for not being willing to spend the money on the two areas. Coloraado's roads have been deteriorating because of the recent population surge.
"You can be a great state. But you can only be a great state if you invest in education, infrastructure and beauty," Romer told a news conference.
Colorado's Taxpayer Bill of Rights, TABOR, limits increases in government spending according to a formula based on the population and the Consumer Price Index. TABOR was passed by voters in 1992.
The state would have to have the voters' permission to spend the $140 million.
Democrats in the legislature initially sided with Romer when the excess figure looked much smaller, but as it grew they changed their minds.
